_note: 1838 Black Metropolis StoryMaps -- five anti-Black mob attacks in Philadelphia (1834, 1835, 1842, 1849, 1871), each its own source. Curated from the StoryMap PDFs in Drive/Newspapers/1838 Research. Each attack becomes an event node; every named person is brought in as source='storymap' (NO auto-linking -- same-name matches like Catto/Purvis/Stephen Smith surface via storymap_matches.md for Michiko's review). Per-person snippet + link to that year's StoryMap. Credit: 1838 Black Metropolis, Michiko Quinones, Morgan Lloyd.

attacks.title: The 1834 "Flying Horses" Mob Attack
attacks.description: A coordinated four-day white-mob terror attack on the Black community, Aug 12-15, 1834, beginning at the Flying Horses carousel at 7th and South. Two Black churches were attacked (one destroyed), over 40 Black homes were wrecked, Stephen James was killed and another man drowned fleeing across the Schuylkill; hundreds sheltered in the woods and in Camden for weeks. Told through the people and what they lost.
people: 50-year-old Stephen James, who had limited mobility due to a prior injury, was beaten by the mob almost to death while his family watched, and died a week later.
Daniel Williamson, age 95 -- an elderly man who had been enslaved by George Washington -- watched helplessly as his two-story house was destroyed.
All the windows and furniture of Charles Akers' three-story brick house were destroyed.
Levin Drake's shoemaker's shop, a two-story building at 209 Shippen, had its windows and furniture destroyed.
217 Shippen, the home of master chimney sweeper John Nicholson, was 'treated with uncommon severity' -- here the mob was particularly destructive.
3 Small Street, belonging to Mr. Fitzgerald, had its windows and furniture destroyed -- 'they left him but one chair and a stove.'
5 Small Street, belonging to Mrs. Moore, had its windows and furniture destroyed.
Mr. Butler's three-story brick house, owned and occupied by Mr. Butler, Mr. Green and two other families, was damaged.
Mr. Green was one of the families living in Mr. Butler's three-story brick house that the mob damaged.
The homes of Samuel Combigbee and Miles White were attacked as the mob moved down Baker's Court.
The homes of Samuel Combigbee and Miles White were attacked as the mob moved down Baker's Court.
Edward Abdy reported that a white Quaker friend of the Black community -- assumed to be Thomas Shipley -- infiltrated the mob and provided intelligence about their plans.
British abolitionist Edward Abdy described how Black people fled for their lives, some living in the woods and fields surrounding the city for weeks.
These events are hinted at in the novel 'The Garies and Their Friends,' written by Frank Webb, who grew up in the Black community.

attacks.title: The 1835 "Red Row" Mob Attack
attacks.description: On July 13, 1835, nearly 1,500 white men attacked the Black community in Moyamensing after a Philadelphia enslaver was nearly killed by the man he enslaved. Philadelphia City police held the mob below South Street, but the Sheriff and military did nothing as the mob burned 'Red Row' and attacked Black homes on Small, Christian and Bainbridge streets. 42 structures damaged, 6 hospitalized, 13 arrested.
people: On July 12, 1835, an Igbo man named Juan nearly killed the Philadelphia enslaver, Stewart, who held him; the press reported Juan may have been manumitted into an indenture toward gradual freedom. The mob attacked the Black community for this act.
A Philadelphia enslaver named Stewart was nearly killed by an Igbo man named Juan, whom he enslaved -- the pretext the white mob used to attack the Black community.
City authorities assembled at Sixth and South under the direction of City Recorder McIlvaine, Mayor Swift and the High Constables, holding the mob below South Street.
City authorities assembled at Sixth and South under the direction of the City Recorder McIlvaine, Mayor Swift and the High Constables.
When the mob beat a Black man who had defended his home with an axe 'with great and cruel severity,' Constable Hofliner prevented the man from being killed.

attacks.title: The 1842 "Lombard Street" Mob Attack
attacks.description: On Aug 1-2, 1842, a white mob attacked a Black temperance procession celebrating West Indian Emancipation Day, then two days of violence that destroyed Beneficial Hall and Second African Presbyterian Church and sent 13 Black people (including a 14-year-old) to the hospital. The attack targeted the flourishing Black temperance movement led by Dr. J.J.G. Bias and the institutions of the Black community.
people: Wealthy lumber and railroad businessman and Black community leader Stephen Smith financed 'Beneficial Hall' to meet the community's need after Pennsylvania Hall burned; after the 1842 attack destroyed it, he sued the City under the Riot Act and won.

Dr. James J.G. Bias was president of the largest Black temperance society, in Moyamensing; his leadership led to over 1,000 members and an estimated 90% drop in rum sales. He lived at 8th and Bedford, near Temperance Hall, which the mob targeted.

The banners carried by the Young Men's Vigilant Association at the rear of the march were designed by Black artist Robert Douglass Junior; one bore a figure pointing to broken chains at his feet and to the word LIBERTY.

Robert Purvis' home at 8th and Lombard came under attack; with his wife and children upstairs, 'Purvis took a seat on the stairs, with his rifle across his knees,' prepared to kill anyone who attacked his family -- a final break with the Garrisonian theory of nonresistance.
Charles Gardner co-wrote 'The Late Riots' (with Robert Purvis and Daniel Payne) documenting the plots laid and cudgels obtained before the attack.
Daniel Payne co-wrote 'The Late Riots' (with Robert Purvis and Charles Gardner) documenting the attack for the Philadelphia Ledger and the Liberator.
A letter from the Wesley Sabbath School agreeing to join the Aug 1 temperance march was addressed to Jacob C. White Sr. (Leon Gardiner Collection, HSP).
Multiple sources say Mayor John Scott was told on the morning of the attack that arson at Beneficial Hall, 7th and Lombard, was planned; the rioters threatened all day to burn the Hall at night.

At Bradford Alley, a teenager named Henry Van Brackle was among three Black people who fought back with gunfire to protect their families; he ran to a rooftop and, with the protection of a policeman named Herman Yerkes, survived getting through the mob to the police station.
Anthony Harvey was among the Black men who fought back with gunfire at Bradford Alley to protect their families; three white men were hit.
A policeman named Herman Yerkes protected the teenager Henry Van Brackle, enabling him to survive getting through the mob to the police station.

Charles Black, a wounded veteran of the War of 1812 who had been sent to English and French prisons because he refused to fight against the United States, was dragged out of his home and beaten along with his son during the attack.
Charles Black, Jr., only 14, was admitted to Pennsylvania Hospital with 'contusions and wound of the scalp' after he and his father were dragged from their home and beaten.
An elderly Black man named Isaac Reed, sawing wood at 10th and Fitzwater, was attacked and beaten by the mob; somehow he made it to the hospital.

At Beneficial Hall, the Sheriff, Judge Todd and the sheriff's men tried to block the mob and reason with them from atop a box, but the mob only yelled and no police appeared before the hall was set ablaze.
Liberator correspondent Henry C. Wright wrote 'The Philadelphia Mob of Aug. 1st, 1842 -- Who Headed It?' documenting the attack.

attacks.title: The 1849 "Boyer House" and "California House" Mob Attacks
attacks.description: Two 1849 mob attacks (the Boyer House defense in August and the California House attack Oct 9-10) in which armed, organized Black self-defense marked a turning point. The Irish 'Killers' gang, tied to Moyamensing police and to General Robert Patterson, attacked Black-owned taverns; Black men defended their spaces, argued self-defense in court and won acquittals. 6 deaths, 10 structures damaged, 17 arrests, $11,000 in damages.
people: Samuel 'Uncle Sammy' Williams owned the Boyer House Tavern at 7th and Lombard, which doubled as an Underground Railroad safehouse; a galvanizing leader for the Black community, he was arrested and acquitted, and later warned Black self-defense organizations in Christiana in 1851.

Benjamin Jackson owned the California House Tavern on St. Mary's Street and was married to a white woman; arrested behind his bar during the attack, he was tried and acquitted on a self-defense argument.
Witnesses saw Black women flee into the Boyer House Tavern during the street battle; Martha Dunlap was later arrested.
Black man William Sammons was arrested at the Boyer House; on the way to the police station, friends who attempted to rescue him were also arrested.
Richard Duncan was among the Black men arrested at the Boyer House Tavern and later found not guilty of rioting.
Jacob Axes was among the Black men arrested when police knocked down the door of Samuel Williams' tavern and found a warm, loaded double-barreled gun.
Alfred Turner was among the Black men arrested at the Boyer House and later found not guilty of rioting.
William Bell was among the Black men arrested at Samuel Williams' Boyer House Tavern.
Three Black men -- James Powell, Elias Thompson and John Petty -- were found guilty of riot after the Boyer House defense.
Three Black men -- James Powell, Elias Thompson and John Petty -- were found guilty of riot after the Boyer House defense.
Three Black men -- James Powell, Elias Thompson and John Petty -- were found guilty of riot after the Boyer House defense.

Counsel Joseph A. Brewster argued self-defense for the Black defendants before Judge Campbell -- and that strategy won acquittals for Benjamin Jackson, Samuel Williams, Alfred Turner and Richard Duncan.
In the Court of Quarter Sessions with Judge Campbell presiding, an all-white jury acquitted the Black tavern defenders after a self-defense argument.

At Mother Bethel AME, one block from the California House fire, member Jane Johnson assembled bags of red pepper, bricks and clubs and instructed the men to run up and down the stairs holding clubs upright so that, in the darkness, they appeared to be guns -- and the mob, afraid, did not attack the church.
A Black young man named Jacob Griffith was shot in the head during the California House attack and later died in the hospital.
Charles Himmelwright of the Good Will fire engine was shot on Sixth Street and carried to a drugstore at Sixth and Lombard, where he died minutes later.
Later testimony named Moyamensing Police Officer James Mayes and Black dog catcher George Horsey as working together to fire multiple rounds at the firemen on Sixth Street.
Later testimony named Black dog catcher George Horsey and Moyamensing Police Officer James Mayes as working together to fire multiple rounds at the firemen.
A white man named Redman Prendible received over ten shots in his back during the Boyer House street battle.
Anna Brady, who lived in the houses across from the tavern, testified that her daughter was hit in the forehead, through the window, with a slug.
An elderly Black man named Isaac M. Cauley suffered a skull fracture from a brick thrown at him at the corner of South and Passyunk.

A Black woman named Anna T. Collins lived on Bedford Street with her husband; when the mob could not find him (he hid under the bed), they set fire to her home. She later found Sheriff Lelar and accused a white man, James Loan, who was arrested.
James Loan, a white man, was arrested after Anna T. Collins accused him of setting fire to her Bedford Street home.
Jonathan Tudas, whose furniture was destroyed by the mob behind the California House, entered an April 1850 suit, won his case and was compensated $35 by the City.
Anna T. Collins found Sheriff Lelar after the mob burned her home and accused the white man James Loan, who was then arrested.

Charles Anderson Chester (street name 'Dick Hellfire') was the leader of the 'Killers'; George Lippard's biography says Chester orchestrated the California House attack as a diversion so he could rob and possibly kill his father Jacob Chester and flee to Cuba.

Lippard portrayed Jacob Chester, father of Killers leader Charles Anderson Chester, as a man whose wealth and activities were tied to human trafficking and coercion; his son planned an attack on the Black community as cover to rob him.

George Lippard's biography of Charles Anderson Chester drew on the later admissions and written statements of Killer James Jones and of Jacob Chester about the planning meeting held the night before the attack.

The Killers had served in the Mexican-American War under General Robert Patterson -- an enslaver who owned plantations and Philadelphia factories -- who was the military commander during the 1849 mob attack and repeatedly marched troops without stationing them to stop the violence.

Henry Silcox's biography of alderman William McMullen documented the Killers' connections to Moyamensing police and pro-slavery interests, echoing national contests over race and enslavement in local attacks on the Black community.
White writer George Lippard authored a sensational 1850 biography of Killers leader Charles Anderson Chester, one of the few sources on the gang's planning and its ties to city corruption.

attacks.title: The 1871 Election Day Mob Attack (Octavius Catto)
attacks.description: A two-day campaign of racial terror on the Oct 1871 election, when newly re-enfranchised Black men voted Republican in numbers that decided the mayoral race. Alderman 'Bull' McMullen's 4th Ward Democratic machine used police and street gangs to suppress the Black vote; 7 people were killed (5 Black men), 30 shot and 47 injured. The murder of Octavius Catto by Frank Kelly was the culmination, not an accident.
people: Octavius Catto, leader of the Pennsylvania Equal Rights League and ICY teacher, closed the school early with Fanny Coppin to get students home safely; returning home at 813 South, he was shot by Frank Kelly, and -- after asking Officer McKnight, 'Mac, give me your protection' -- was shot again in the back into the heart and died at the Fifth District station.

Frank Kelly, a McMullen operative, led a crowd terrorizing residents, killed Isaac Chase, shot at John Fawcett and Rev. Asbury Smith, and then murdered Octavius Catto -- part of the 4th Ward Democratic machine's terror unit, not a lone operative.

40-year-old stevedore Jacob Gordon, a Ward 4 resident, was chased and shot in the back on election eve; he collapsed at his home at 713 Russell Street and died two days later, first identifying his shooter as Officer McNulty, a known Bull McMullen operative.

Moses Wright was shot in the back on election eve, made it to the hospital and was discharged; on October 19 his body was pulled from the Delaware River at Pier 5 -- a suspicious drowning, as he may have witnessed Jacob Gordon's murder.

Levi Bolden, a U.S. Colored Troop veteran who with his wife Mary Ann had lost an infant that year, was standing at 7th and St. Mary when uniformed Police Sergeant James Duffy shot him; he was admitted to Penn Hospital and died on October 23.

Isaac Chase, a 30-year-old musician, husband to Sarah Ellen and father of two, left his house to draw the mob away from his children; Frank Kelly's crew crashed his gate and shot him in the back in the alley -- witnessed by his daughter Julia -- then crushed his head with a hatchet.

George Dougherty, a white Democratic election officer who had worked the 6th and Lombard poll window, was killed the day after the election; reports conflict, but Black residents said the bullet was fired in self-defense as his group shot at Black homes on Cullen (Bradford) street.
William Bramwell, described in Pennsylvania Hospital records as a 'mendicant' and most likely unhoused, died on October 12 during the election violence; the record says he died of 'violence.'

Black leaders built organizations like the Social, Civil and Statistical Association, led by Isaiah C. Wears, William Still and Jonathan Gibbs; Wears, a former SCSA president, was invited to Washington in 1870 to help the House Judiciary Committee draft language for the 15th Amendment.

The Social, Civil and Statistical Association, led by Isaiah C. Wears, William Still and Jonathan Gibbs, was one of the Black organizations fighting for the vote and headquartered in the 7th and Lombard area.
Jonathan Gibbs helped lead the Social, Civil and Statistical Association (with Isaiah C. Wears and William Still), one of the Black organizations fighting for Black suffrage in Philadelphia.

The Pennsylvania Equal Rights League, headquartered at 717 Lombard, was led by Jacob C. White Jr. and Octavius Catto; Catto stopped to see White at 7th and Lombard on election day, reporting he had implored the mayor to protect voters.

Incumbent Democratic Mayor Daniel Fox was defeated by Republican William Stokely by about 8,000 votes, a few thousand of them Black men; during the violence he was slow to call the military and clashed publicly with Judge Allison over charging Lieutenant Haggarty.
Republican challenger William Stokely defeated incumbent Mayor Daniel Fox by about 8,000 votes, a margin that included a few thousand newly enfranchised Black men.

Democratic 4th Ward Alderman William 'Bull' McMullen held deep control of police and fire departments and was staunchly anti-Black; his machine organized the terror unit -- including Frank Kelly and Reddy Dever -- that suppressed the Black vote and was tied to three of the day's killings.
Reddy Dever, with Frank Kelly, led a crowd out of Bull McMullen's saloon onto Emeline to terrorize residents, first attacking Margaret Barrett's home and then forcing their way toward Isaac Chase's.
Officer Edward McNulty, a known Bull McMullen operative, was identified by the dying Jacob Gordon as the man who shot him in the back on election eve.
Uniformed Police Sergeant James Duffy shot USCT veteran Levi Bolden at 7th and St. Mary; Bolden died at Penn Hospital on October 23.

Lieutenant Haggarty was in charge as Henry Lewis was shot in the hand and was later identified by Black and white witnesses as one of the officers obstructing the polls; Judge Allison issued a warrant and he was held on $10,000 bail.
Henry Lewis was pulled out of the voting line and shot in the hand by police while Lieutenant Haggarty was in charge.
An oral-history account, printed in the Philadelphia Tribune years later, recalled that Edward Hall, a stevedore, punched Bull McMullen during a poll encounter.
Judge Allison issued a warrant for the arrest of Lieutenant Haggarty for obstructing the polls and had a heated public exchange with Mayor Fox over whether to entertain the charges.

John Fawcett was chased and shot at by Frank Kelly's group; he dodged into the cellar of a stove store whose owner, Harry Burrichter, quickly closed the cellar doors -- Fawcett survived, kept the bullet, and later testified against Frank Kelly at trial.
Harry Burrichter, the owner of a stove store, thought quickly and closed his cellar doors to hide John Fawcett from Frank Kelly's pursuing crew, saving his life.

Frank Kelly and his crew shot at Rev. Asbury Smith on 8th near Bainbridge; Smith ran down Bainbridge, turned down Lisle (Mildred) and escaped -- moments before Kelly turned onto South Street and killed Catto.
As a wounded Catto approached Officer McKnight -- 'Mac,' he said, 'give me your protection' -- and turned his back to Frank Kelly, the final shots were fired; McKnight caught Catto as he fell.
Frank Kelly and Reddy Dever's crowd first attacked Margaret Barrett's home on Emeline before forcing their way toward Isaac Chase's alley.
Isaac Chase's shooting in the back was witnessed by his 10-year-old daughter Julia, who provided testimony just a few days later at the coroner's inquest.
Octavius Catto and Fanny Coppin decided to close the Institute for Colored Youth early on election day to ensure the students returned home safely.
The National Equal Rights League, of which Philadelphia's PERL was part, was founded in 1864 by Henry Highland Garnet, Frederick Douglass and John Mercer Langston.
